intro: The noise grain texture generator layers an SVG turbulence filter over a two-color gradient to show how grain removes banding and adds a printed texture.
content:
- The noise grain texture generator takes two colours and one action: choose a From and a To, and a fine grain appears over the gradient between them.
- There are no sliders for the grain, no opacity control and no code output — the page demonstrates the combination and leaves the implementation to you.

The technique it shows is worth understanding, because it is the standard answer to a common problem. A gradient painted across a large area in eight bits per channel rarely renders smoothly: the browser has to fit a continuous ramp into a limited number of steps, and where adjacent steps are far enough apart to be visible the result is banding — soft, contour-like lines running across the surface. Adding noise breaks the contours up. The eye stops resolving the steps because the noise dominates the local contrast, and the gradient reads as continuous even though the underlying values have not changed.

The grain in the preview is an SVG filter, not an image. A turbulence element with a high base frequency and two octaves generates fractal noise procedurally, and it is drawn in a rectangle filling the panel, layered over the gradient at reduced opacity with an overlay blend mode. Being generated rather than loaded has two consequences: it costs no network request, and it stays crisp at any size because it is computed rather than stretched. The high frequency is what makes it read as grain rather than as clouds — a lower frequency would produce blotches instead.

Reproducing the effect in your own work is a matter of keeping the gradient and adding the overlay. The base is an ordinary linear gradient, and the grain is that same SVG rect placed over it with absolute positioning, partial opacity and a blend mode. If the grain itself needs to be a CSS background, the equivalent approach is a small tiling SVG or a base64-encoded noise image repeated as a background layer — the same idea with a different plumbing.

Where grain is worth the extra layer is anywhere a gradient covers a large area: hero backgrounds, full-width banners, presentation slides and email headers. It is also a way to give flat colour a printed or photographic feel without changing the colour, which is why it turns up in editorial and brand work. And it helps with another artefact of the same family — a gradient that passes through a very similar pair of colours can show visible steps even though the total range is small, and noise fixes that case too.

- There is no code output on this page, so the recipe has to be transcribed rather than copied.
- The grain amount, scale and opacity are fixed, so it cannot be tuned to a surface or to a print size.
- The texture cannot be exported on its own.
- Because the SVG filter is rendered live by the browser, the exact appearance of the noise varies a little between engines.

Used as a way to see what grain does to a pair of colours, the tool does its job in one step. As a reference for the technique — how to add grain to gradient artwork with an svg noise texture and a noise overlay css blend — it shows the correct construction, and the resulting grainy gradient is the right answer whenever banding is showing on a large smooth surface.
howTo: Set the From and To colours to the gradient you are working with.
Look at the preview to see how grain changes the way the ramp reads.
Reproduce it in your own work by keeping the gradient and adding the noise layer over it.
whenToUse: Use this when a gradient will be large enough for banding to show, or when flat colour needs a printed texture. Use a plain gradient builder when the surface is small enough that grain is unnecessary. Where the same pair should be shown without any texture, the {{linear-gradient-generator|linear gradient generator}} is the plain version; where the noise is one of several treatments on the same element, the {{css-filter-generator|CSS filter generator}} covers the other filter-based ones — blur, brightness, contrast, saturation and hue-rotate — that stack with a noise layer.

faqs.q: What does the grain actually do?
faqs.a: It breaks up the visible steps a gradient shows when a smooth ramp is fitted into eight bits per channel. The noise dominates the local contrast, so the eye reads the surface as continuous.

faqs.q: Is the noise an image file?
faqs.a: No. It is an SVG turbulence filter generated by the browser, so there is no download cost and the grain stays consistent at any size.

faqs.q: Can I change how strong the grain is?
faqs.a: Not on this page — the amount, frequency and opacity are fixed, and there is no code output to copy. The construction shown is what you would reproduce with your own values.

faqs.q: Will the grain look identical everywhere?
faqs.a: Not exactly. The filter is rendered by each browser engine, so the fine detail varies slightly between them.

faqs.q: Can the grain sit over a flat colour instead of a gradient?
faqs.a: Yes — the turbulence layer is independent of what it sits on, so the same recipe over a solid fill gives the same speckle. The blend does react to the colour underneath, so the grain takes on that colour rather than the gradient's.

intro: The gradient to CSS exporter writes a finished gradient three ways at once — the background shorthand, the explicit background-image property and a custom property — so it can be dropped into an existing stylesheet.
content:
- The controls are the familiar stop and angle set; the panel at the bottom holds three declarations rather than one.
- All three describe the same gradient in the same notation, and differ only in how a stylesheet consumes them.
- The copy button takes all three together, so nothing has to be retyped.

The first line is the background shorthand, which is what most people reach for: one property, the gradient, done. The second repeats the identical value as background-image, which exists for a specific situation. The shorthand resets every background property it does not mention — position, size, repeat, attachment, origin, clip — so assigning a gradient with it can quietly undo a background position set elsewhere in the same rule. Using the longhand changes only the image and leaves the rest of the background stack intact. That distinction causes real bugs in stylesheets where a gradient is layered onto an existing background, and having both spellings side by side is the simplest way to avoid it.

The third line is a custom property holding the gradient value, which is the form worth understanding if you have not used it. Declaring a gradient once as a variable and referencing it from several rules means the palette can be changed in one place: a hover state, a themed variant and a fallback can all point at the same definition instead of repeating the stops. It also lets the gradient be assembled from other custom properties, so the stops themselves can vary by theme while the gradient expression stays fixed. The trade is that a custom property containing a gradient is only meaningful where it is consumed, so the declaration needs to sit somewhere both the definition and the use can see.

Which form you want depends on what you are doing with it. Copying into a fresh rule, the shorthand is fine. Editing a rule that already positions a background, the longhand is safer. Building a theme where several components share one treatment, the custom property is the right starting point. Because all three arrive together, the decision is made after copying rather than before, and there is no risk of the three drifting apart since they are generated from the same state.

The controls themselves cover what the rest of the cluster covers: any number of stops with individual colour and position sliders, and an angle from zero to three hundred and sixty degrees, with the angle always written in degrees rather than as a direction keyword. It is a linear gradient throughout — radial and conic are not produced here — and no vendor prefixes are added, since gradients have been unprefixed in every current browser for years.

Used as a gradient to css exporter, then, this is the page for getting a gradient into a stylesheet in whichever shape the stylesheet needs. Where the angle adjuster is about choosing the gradient, this one is about delivering it: three spellings, one copy, no retyping, and the copy gradient css code arrives ready for whichever of the three the rule can actually accept. Whether the rule wants the css gradient shorthand, the explicit background-image property, or a gradient custom property that several selectors can share, the export gradient css step is already done.
howTo: Set the stops and the angle until the preview looks right.
Copy the block — three declarations come together.
Keep the shorthand for a fresh rule, the background-image line when a rule already sets background position or size.
Use the custom property line when several rules should share one gradient definition.
whenToUse: Use this when a gradient is being moved into a stylesheet and the form matters — layered backgrounds, theming, or several components sharing one treatment. Use the SVG or canvas generators when the destination is not CSS. When the gradient becomes one of many values a theme has to carry, the {{css-custom-properties-exporter|CSS custom properties exporter}} writes the whole variable block, and the {{design-token-generator|design token generator}} takes the same values into a token file.

faqs.q: Why are three declarations produced instead of one?
faqs.a: They are the same gradient written for three situations: the shorthand for a fresh rule, background-image when a rule already sets other background properties, and a custom property for sharing one definition across rules.

faqs.q: When does the shorthand cause a problem?
faqs.a: It resets every background property it does not mention, including position, size and repeat. If a rule already layers a gradient over a positioned background, the longhand is the safer choice.

faqs.q: What is the custom property line for?
faqs.a: Sharing one gradient across several rules or themes. Declare it once and reference it wherever the gradient is used, so changing the stops changes every use.

faqs.q: Are browser prefixes included?
faqs.a: No. Modern browsers support gradients unprefixed, so the output is the declaration alone.

faqs.q: Can I copy just one of the three lines?
faqs.a: Only by selecting it by hand — the copy button takes the whole block. That is the right default for pasting into a file that wants all three, and a single line is a quick manual trim when a file needs only one of them.

keywords: mix two colors into a palette
intro: The gradient palette mixer blends two endpoint colors into a fixed five-swatch palette taken at even intervals, so the colours between them can be used as flat values.
content:
- The gradient palette mixer takes a From colour and a To colour and lays out five swatches: the two endpoints and three colours evenly spaced between them.
- Each swatch shows its hex value with a copy button, and the row recalculates as either colour changes.
- That is the whole tool — two inputs, five outputs, no further settings.

The positions are the thing to notice, because they are fixed rather than adjustable. The five swatches sit at zero, twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five and a hundred percent of the distance from one endpoint to the other. That is a quarter-step ladder, which is why the set behaves like a small scale rather than a freeform blend: there is always a colour exactly halfway between the two ends, and always one a quarter of the way along. If you need a different number of steps or a different spacing, the gradient interpolator in this domain offers between three and fifteen, and the stop editor lets positions be placed by hand.

What the fixed quarter steps are good for is palette work in a design file. A five-swatch strip is small enough to read at a glance, large enough to give you a light, a mid and a dark option in a family, and consistent between projects because the spacing never changes. Adding a border, a hover state and a disabled state to a component usually means reaching for three related tones of one colour, and a quarter-step ladder supplies them without any decisions about where to put the intermediate values.

The blending itself is a straight line through the red, green and blue channels, which is the simplest interpolation and not always the most attractive. Neighbouring hues come out smooth — blending a teal into a blue gives a convincing family — while complementary pairs sag in the middle, because the straight line between them passes close to neutral. A mid blue and a red, for instance, meet at a muted violet that is noticeably duller than either endpoint. Knowing this is mostly about prediction: if a strip looks flat in the centre, the endpoints are probably too far apart on the wheel, and moving one slightly improves the result more than anything else.

There is no gradient in the output, and that is deliberate. The tool returns discrete colours with individual copy buttons, which is what a palette needs — chart series, category colours, tags and swatch libraries cannot accept a continuous ramp. If the goal is a painted ramp instead, that is a gradient tool; if the goal is five usable values that belong together, this is the shorter route.

Limits: exactly five swatches, no step control, no interpolation-space option, and no export beyond copying the hex values one at a time.

- It also does not check contrast, so a pair that works as a palette may not work as text on a surface.
- Used to mix two colors into a palette, though, it does the one thing quickly, and as a two color palette generator it produces a five color blend that is immediately usable as a color blend palette for an interface.
howTo: Set the From colour — usually the darker or more neutral of the two.
Set the To colour and read the five swatches as a quarter-step ladder.
Copy the individual hex values into your palette, or use the endpoints as accents and the middle values as surfaces.
whenToUse: Use this when you need a small, fixed palette derived from two colours — component states, chart series, a swatch strip. Use the interpolator when the number of steps needs to vary, or a gradient generator when the output should be a painted ramp. For a ramp that has to pass through a third colour rather than straight between two, the {{multi-stop-gradient-builder|multi-stop gradient builder}} extends the same interpolation with real stop positions, and a set built from one hue rather than a pair is what the {{monochromatic-palette-generator|monochromatic palette generator}} produces.

faqs.q: How many colours does it produce?
faqs.a: Five — the two endpoints plus three evenly spaced colours at 25, 50 and 75 percent of the blend. The spacing is fixed.

faqs.q: Can I change the number of steps?
faqs.a: Not on this page. The gradient interpolator offers between three and fifteen steps, and the stop editor allows hand-placed positions.

faqs.q: Why does the middle look dull for some pairs?
faqs.a: The blend is a straight line through the RGB channels. Complementary pairs pass close to neutral halfway along and lose saturation; neighbouring hues blend cleanly.

faqs.q: Is the output a gradient?
faqs.a: No, it is five discrete colours with copy buttons. That is the point — charts, legends and design files take individual values rather than a ramp.

faqs.q: Can the same two colours produce a dark-mode counterpart?
faqs.a: Not from here — there is no lightness inversion and the five steps are fixed to the two values you set. A dark version means choosing darker endpoints and letting the mixer fill the three steps between them.

intro: The gradient collection browser presents twelve ready-made two-color gradients with their hex pairs and a one-click copy of each as a CSS background declaration.
content:
- The gradient collection browser lays twelve gradients out in a responsive grid, three across on a wide screen.
- Each entry is a card with the gradient rendered across the top and its two hex values beneath, shown as one arrow to the other.
- The copy button on a card takes the full declaration rather than just the colours, so one click puts a usable background into the clipboard.

The set covers a wide spread of colour relationships on purpose. There are warm sunset pairs, such as a red-orange running into a deep pink, and a yellow-gold into a burnt orange. There are cool pairs, including a deep navy into a bright cyan, and a sky blue into a saturated blue. There are the more stylised combinations — a violet into magenta, a dark purple into a muted mauve, an aqua into a vivid green — and there are deliberately subdued options, such as a near-black into a slate blue, for when a gradient should sit behind content rather than compete with it. That range is the point of a preset library: between them, the twelve cover the moods most projects actually need.

Every gradient in the collection is drawn on the same diagonal, one hundred and thirty-five degrees, which runs from top left to bottom right. Fixing the angle is a sensible choice for a browser, because it makes the presets comparable to one another — you are judging the colour pairing, not the direction — and it means every copied declaration has the same shape, so swapping one preset for another in a stylesheet is a one-line change.

The workflow is deliberately short. Scroll the grid, find the pair that matches the mood, and either copy the declaration as-is or copy it and edit the ones you want to keep. Because the card shows the two hex values beside the preview, it doubles as a way to lift just one colour out of a gradient: read the code, take it to a format converter, and use it as a flat colour elsewhere. That is often the more useful outcome, since a pair that works as a gradient is frequently a pair that works as an accent and a surface.

Being clear about what it is not: a browser, not a builder. Nothing here is editable, and there is no search, filtering or sorting — the twelve are presented as a fixed grid in a fixed order. Nor is it a searchable library in the sense of hundreds of entries: it is a small curated set, which is a reasonable trade, because a page of twelve gradients is browsable at a glance while a page of two hundred is a search problem. If you want to generate a gradient from your own colours, a builder is the right tool; if you want to modify one of these, the angle adjuster and the stop editor both accept the same syntax.

Used as a source of css gradient presets, then, this is a fast route from a blank backdrop to something finished: browse css gradients, copy gradient css, and adjust afterwards if needed. As a gradient library it is small on purpose, and as a starting point for a hero background, an avatar placeholder or a card header it covers more ground than its twelve entries suggest.
howTo: Scroll the grid and pick the pair whose mood matches what you need.
Read the two hex values on the card if you only want one of the colours.
Press copy to take the full background declaration, including the angle and both stops.
Adjust the angle or the stops in a gradient builder if the preset needs adapting.
whenToUse: Use this when you want a finished gradient quickly and are happy to work from an existing pair of colours. Use a gradient generator when the colours come from your own palette, or the image gradient tool when they should come from a photograph. A preset whose stops or angle need moving is the {{gradient-color-stop-editor|gradient color stop editor}}'s job, and a ramp that has to be delivered as a file rather than a declaration is what the {{css-gradient-to-image-exporter|CSS gradient to image exporter}} writes out.

faqs.q: Can I edit a preset?
faqs.a: Not on this page. The collection is read-only, but you can paste the copied declaration into a gradient builder and change the stops or the angle there.

faqs.q: Why are all the gradients on the same diagonal?
faqs.a: Every preset uses 135 degrees, running from top left to bottom right. Keeping the angle constant makes the twelve comparable and the copied declarations interchangeable.

faqs.q: How do I use just one of the two colours?
faqs.a: Each card prints both hex values, so you can copy one into a colour field or a converter and use it as a flat colour instead of a gradient.

faqs.q: Is there a search or filter?
faqs.a: No. The twelve presets appear as a fixed grid. The set is deliberately small enough to scan rather than search.

faqs.q: How do I get just the two hex values from a card?
faqs.a: Read them off the card — they are printed as one arrow to the other. The copy button takes the whole background value, so trimming to the pair is a manual selection when that is all you are after.

intro: The gradient angle calculator converts a degree value into every equivalent form a gradient direction can take — degrees, turns, radians and the nearest direction keyword — with a dial showing which way it points.
content:
- The gradient angle calculator pairs an angle slider with a circular dial whose line rotates to show the direction.
- To the right, an Equivalents panel gives four rows for the same angle: degrees, turns, radians, and the nearest CSS direction keyword.
- Everything updates as the slider moves.

The reason there are four rows rather than one is that CSS accepts all four forms for the same direction, and they arrive from different places. Degrees come from design tools and the angle slider in a gradient builder. Turns come from animation and design documentation, where a value like a quarter turn is easier to reason about than ninety degrees. Radians come out of calculation functions and geometry code. And keywords come from hand-written CSS, where to bottom right is both readable and unambiguous. Having the table in front of you removes the arithmetic, and the degrees row is formatted so the value can be pasted directly into a gradient declaration.

The nearest keyword row is the part with a real decision inside it. There are only eight keywords in common use — to top, to top right, to right, to bottom right, to bottom, to bottom left, to left and to top left — so they sit forty-five degrees apart around the circle, and any angle between two of them has to resolve to one or the other. The tool finds the closest by measuring the circular distance between the angle and each of the eight, normalising first so that anything at or above a full turn wraps around properly. That normalisation is what makes three hundred and sixty degrees resolve to to top rather than to to top left, and it is the detail that a naive implementation gets wrong, because an unwrapped angle is the largest possible distance from zero rather than the same direction as it.

Degrees and radians deserve a note about what the conversion means. Radians are the mathematically natural unit — a full circle is two pi — so a quarter turn is a value a bit above one and a half, and the rounded figures here are meant for reading rather than for computing. If you are writing a calculation, use the exact expression rather than a rounded decimal.

The dial is drawn the way CSS measures: the line rotates by the angle minus ninety degrees, because the reference line starts pointing right while zero degrees in CSS points up. That makes this a gradient angle to keyword conversion at a glance as well as a numeric one. That offset is easy to get wrong by hand and is the reason a direction you set in a builder sometimes comes out rotated ninety degrees when you transcribe it into a diagram.

What the tool does not do is generate a gradient — it converts and explains, and the angles it reports are the ones you feed to a builder.

- It does not generate a gradient — it converts and explains angles, so a ramp still needs a builder.
- It only knows the eight keywords, so an angle of, say, twenty-two degrees reports the nearest of them rather than the direction it actually points to.
- Used as a css gradient direction reference, though, it answers the question that comes up constantly when reading other people's stylesheets, and as a degrees to turn css and gradient direction converter it covers all four spellings in one view.
howTo: Move the slider to the angle you are working with, or read it off an existing gradient.
Read the dial to confirm which way that direction points on screen.
Take the equivalent you need — degrees for a declaration, turns or radians for documentation.
Use the nearest keyword row when you want the readable form in your CSS.
whenToUse: Use this when translating a gradient direction between degrees, turns, radians and keywords, or when checking which way an angle points. Use the gradient angle adjuster when you need to build the gradient itself rather than convert its direction. When the answer has to become a gradient rather than a number, the {{gradient-angle-adjuster|gradient angle adjuster}} is the same slider with stops attached, and a ramp that needs flipping without being rebuilt is what the {{gradient-reverser|gradient reverser}} does.

faqs.q: Why does the dial line point to the right at 0 degrees?
faqs.a: Because the reference line starts horizontal while zero degrees in CSS points up. The line is rotated by the angle minus ninety to compensate, which is why 0 degrees shows it pointing up on the dial.

faqs.q: How are the direction keywords spaced?
faqs.a: There are eight of them, forty-five degrees apart. An angle between two keywords reports whichever is nearer, measured as circular distance so values near 360 resolve correctly.

faqs.q: How many turns is 90 degrees?
faqs.a: A quarter — the panel reports it in decimals, so ninety degrees reads as 0.250 turn, alongside about 1.571 radians.

faqs.q: Can I get an exact direction rather than a keyword?
faqs.a: Only the eight common keywords are covered, so an unusual angle reports the closest of them rather than a custom name. The degrees row always gives the precise value.

faqs.q: Can I paste the turns or radians row straight into CSS?
faqs.a: Yes — CSS accepts all three units in a gradient function, so 90deg, 0.25turn and 1.5708rad are the same direction written three ways. The keyword row is the one that only applies inside a gradient, since direction keywords are not valid anywhere else.

intro: The CSS gradient to image exporter renders your gradient onto a real canvas and downloads it as a 1200 by 800 PNG, with no code to copy and nothing uploaded.
content:
- The controls are the standard stop-and-angle set with a live preview; the code panel is replaced by a single action.
- A Download PNG button sits beside a note stating the size of the file it produces, and pressing it saves a twelve-hundred by eight-hundred PNG of the gradient shown above.

The generation happens entirely in the page. On click, the tool creates a canvas in memory at the full output size, computes the gradient axis from the current angle, adds one colour stop per entry in the ramp with its position converted into the range the canvas API expects, paints a rectangle covering the surface, and turns the result into a data URL. That is then handed to a download link and triggered. Nothing leaves the browser: there is no upload step, no server round trip and no third party involved, which matters if the gradient is part of unreleased work.

The resolution is fixed at twelve hundred by eight hundred, which is roughly the shape of a wide hero or a presentation slide and comfortably above the size most screenshots and headers need. Because the gradient is rebuilt at that size rather than scaled up from the preview, the result is a clean, smooth surface with no interpolation artefacts — the same reason a gradient is a poor candidate for upscaling an existing bitmap and a good candidate for being drawn fresh at the size you need.

- The axis geometry changes shape with the angle even though the canvas dimensions never do: the ramp is drawn along a line stretched to span the whole rectangle in the chosen direction.
- A ninety-degree angle therefore produces a strictly horizontal ramp across the width, while a forty-five-degree angle runs corner to corner and covers a longer distance than the width alone.
- The result matches how a browser paints the same declaration, so the preview and the file agree.

Where an image is the right deliverable rather than a declaration: an email header, where support for gradients is unreliable and an image is the safe option; a social card or open-graph image; a slide background; a placeholder that has to sit somewhere CSS cannot reach. An exported gradient background image png also removes any dependence on browser gradient rendering, so the file looks identical everywhere it is used.

What it does not offer: no size control, so you take twelve hundred by eight hundred or generate elsewhere; no JPEG or WebP output; no transparent variant, since the gradient fills the frame; and no SVG export, which is the other vector route and lives on its own page here. It also only exports a linear gradient, in keeping with the rest of this cluster. Within those bounds, when the question is how to go from a css gradient to image file with as few steps as possible, this is one button: pick the colours, choose the angle, and download gradient image as a png. Converting a CSS gradient to an image by hand usually means recreating it in a graphics editor; here the browser does the rendering, so gradient to png is a single click and there is no redrawing to get out of step with the original. If the task is to export gradient as image for an email or a slide, that is exactly the workflow this page supports.
howTo: Set the stop colours and positions, then choose the angle.
Check the preview, remembering the exported file is drawn at the same angle and proportions.
Press Download PNG to save a 1200 × 800 image.
whenToUse: Use this when the gradient has to exist as a file — email headers, social cards, slide backgrounds, places where CSS gradients are unreliable. Use the CSS or SVG exporters when the gradient can stay a declaration or vector markup. When it is allowed to stay a declaration, the {{gradient-to-css-exporter|gradient to CSS exporter}} hands it back in three stylesheet forms; when it should stay vector, the {{svg-gradient-generator|SVG gradient generator}} writes the markup instead.

faqs.q: What size is the PNG?
faqs.a: 1200 × 800 pixels, drawn at that size rather than scaled from the preview. There is no control for changing it.

faqs.q: Is anything uploaded?
faqs.a: No. The image is rendered in the browser on a local canvas and handed to a download link, so the pixels never leave your machine.

faqs.q: Can I export a JPEG or an SVG instead?
faqs.a: Not here — the output is PNG only. The SVG gradient generator produces vector markup if that is what you need.

faqs.q: Does the angle change the file dimensions?
faqs.a: No, the canvas is always the same size; only the direction of the ramp changes. A diagonal angle therefore covers more distance across the same rectangle.

faqs.q: Is the exported PNG transparent?
faqs.a: No — the whole twelve-hundred by eight-hundred rectangle is filled with the ramp, so the file is fully opaque and can be dropped onto any background. A transparent edge would have to be added afterwards in an image editor.

intro: The gradient from image tool clusters an uploaded photograph into five dominant colors and lays them out as a horizontal five-stop gradient, returning the CSS ready to paste.
content:
The gradient from image tool is one upload and one result. Drop a picture onto the dropzone and the page reads its colours, then draws a horizontal gradient from them and prints the CSS declaration beneath with a copy button. A Replace image button resets the state. There are no settings — the number of colours and the direction are both fixed.

The colours come from clustering rather than sampling. The image is shrunk to a small working size and its pixels are grouped into five clusters by similarity, each cluster represented by its average colour. That is a more interesting answer than picking five pixels at random, because clustering finds the colours that actually account for large areas of the image rather than the ones that happen to sit under a particular coordinate. A photograph of a coastline comes back with sky, sea and sand rather than with five near-identical shades of blue.

The five resulting colours then become the stops of a linear gradient running left to right, spaced evenly at zero, twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five and a hundred percent. Even spacing is deliberate: it makes the output predictable and easy to read, and it keeps the attention on the colours themselves. If a particular colour needs more of the ramp, the declaration is plain CSS and the percentages can be rewritten by hand afterwards.

One property of the output is worth anticipating. The stops are ordered by cluster index, not by lightness, so the resulting gradient is not necessarily a ramp from dark to light — it may go from a mid blue to a dark green to a pale sand and back. That is a faithful representation of the photograph, and a poor match for situations where you want a tonal progression. If the goal is a scale, sort the five hexes by lightness before using them.

On determinism, the clustering is seeded at fixed positions rather than randomly, which means the same image produces the same five colours every time. Uploading the same file twice will not give you two different palettes, and neither will a page reload. That is the behaviour you want from a tool whose output is destined for a stylesheet — a colour that changes between runs is a bug rather than a feature.

Where this is most useful is when an interface has to agree with an image. A hero section, a card, an email header: taking the gradient from the photograph means the treatment is guaranteed to be in the picture's palette rather than near it, and it removes the guesswork from matching. It is also a fast way to get a decorative background that has some relationship to the content, rather than a preset chosen at random — an image color gradient that came from the asset itself, so the two always agree.

- Limits worth noting: five colours and ninety degrees are fixed, transparent pixels are ignored when sampling, and clustering compresses the image's subtler shades into five representatives.
- There is no way to weight one region over another — the whole frame participates.
- Within those bounds, to create gradient from photo without leaving the browser is one upload away, and as a way to extract gradient from picture content into a photo based gradient css declaration it removes the colour matching step entirely.
howTo: Drop an image onto the upload area.
Read the resulting five-colour gradient, remembering the stops follow cluster order rather than lightness.
Copy the background declaration and paste it into your stylesheet.
Reorder or re-space the stops by hand if you want a tonal ramp instead.
whenToUse: Use this when a component needs to take its colours from a photograph — hero banners, image cards, email headers. Use the palette extractor when you want the image's colours as discrete swatches rather than as a gradient, or the dominant colour finder for a single value. A set of discrete swatches rather than a ramp is what the {{color-palette-extractor|color palette extractor}} returns, and a single representative value is the {{dominant-color-finder|dominant color finder}}'s answer.

faqs.q: How many colours does it use?
faqs.a: Five, found by clustering the image's pixels into five groups and taking each group's average. Both the count and the 90 degree direction are fixed.

faqs.q: Is the result the same every time?
faqs.a: Yes. The clustering is seeded deterministically, so the same image produces the same five colours on every upload and after every reload.

faqs.q: Why is the gradient not light to dark?
faqs.a: Because the stops follow cluster order rather than brightness. If you want a tonal progression, sort the five hex values by lightness and reorder the stops in the declaration.

faqs.q: Can I use this for a whole photograph?
faqs.a: The tool produces a five-colour abstraction of the image, not a reproduction. It works well as a background treatment derived from a photograph rather than as a replacement for it.

faqs.q: What happens to the transparent parts of an image?
faqs.a: They are skipped when the image is sampled, so a cut-out logo or a PNG with a clear background contributes no colour to the five stops — only the visible areas vote.

intro: The image theme generator clusters an uploaded image into six colors and assigns them to interface roles — background, surface, primary, secondary, accent and foreground.
content:
- One upload returns six swatches, each with a role name above it and its hex value below: background, surface, primary, secondary, accent and foreground.
- The colours are grouped by similarity rather than picked one by one.
- A Replace image button resets the state, and there are no settings.

Clustering is what makes the output usable rather than arbitrary. Rather than picking six pixels, the tool groups the image's pixels by similarity so that each of the six results represents a genuine region of colour — enough sky, enough foliage, enough of whatever dominates. On a landscape, that tends to produce several related greens and blues with one warm note, which is a far better starting point than six random samples would be.

The role labels are the part to approach with care, and understanding how they are assigned saves a lot of confusion. The six clusters come out of the algorithm in an order determined by how the clustering seeds, and the labels are applied to that order positionally — the first cluster is called background, the second surface, and so on down to foreground. Nothing in the process looks at whether a colour is dark enough to be a background or light enough to be readable as text. So the swatch labelled foreground may well be a mid-tone that cannot be read on the swatch labelled background, and the one labelled background may be the most vivid colour in the picture.

That is a real limitation, and it is best treated as a starting point rather than a finished theme. The useful move is to read the six values, then decide the roles yourself: sort them by lightness, put the darkest where text or a border belongs, the lightest under the largest surface, and keep one vivid colour as the accent. Running a contrast check between whichever pair you settle on for text and surface is the essential next step, since a palette that looks cohesive is not automatically legible.

A second property worth knowing is determinism. The clustering is seeded at fixed positions rather than randomly, so the same image produces the same six colours every time — on a reload, on a second upload, on a different day. For something whose output is destined for a stylesheet, that stability is important: a theme that shifts between runs would be unusable.

Where this fits is at the start of a design rather than the end. A product built around photography — a travel app, a recipe site, a portfolio — can take its palette from its own imagery, which guarantees that the interface and the pictures agree instead of merely coexisting. The six clusters are usually enough to establish a tonal hierarchy without inventing anything, and having the colours come from the content removes the usual round of subjective argument.

- Limits worth naming: six colours and six fixed labels, no control over the count, no contrast checking, no export beyond copying individual swatches, and a bias towards whatever covers the most area — so a small but vivid detail may not survive clustering at all.
- There is no way to generate theme from image with one region weighted over another; the whole frame participates equally.
- Used as an image theme generator, it answers build palette from image in one upload, and with the labels reassigned to match how the interface is actually built the result is a ui theme from photo that is at least guaranteed to be an image color scheme drawn from the picture itself.
howTo: Drop an image onto the upload area.
Read the six swatches and their hex values.
Reassign the role labels yourself — sort by lightness and reserve the most vivid colour as the accent.
Check contrast between the text and surface pairings you intend to use.
whenToUse: Use this when a project's palette should come from its own imagery — photography-led products, portfolios, editorial layouts. Use the palette extractor when you want the colours without interface roles attached, or the dominant colour finder for a single value. Since the roles arrive unchecked, the {{palette-accessibility-checker|palette accessibility checker}} is where the pairs a real interface depends on get audited, and a wider set derived from one of the swatches is what the {{single-color-to-full-palette|single color to full palette}} builds.

faqs.q: How are the roles decided?
faqs.a: Positionally — the six clusters come out of the algorithm in an order and the labels are applied to that order. No colour property is checked, so the labels are suggestions rather than judgements.

faqs.q: Is the result accessible?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. There is no contrast checking, and a swatch labelled foreground may not be readable on the one labelled background. Test any pairing you intend to ship.

faqs.q: Does the same image give the same theme?
faqs.a: Yes. The clustering is seeded deterministically, so the six colours are identical on every upload and after every reload.

faqs.q: How many colours are produced?
faqs.a: Six, always. The count is fixed, and there is no control over how the clusters are formed.

faqs.q: Can I rename or reassign a role after the fact?
faqs.a: Not on the page — the six labels are fixed, and the roles are names attached to the clustered values rather than a mapping you can edit. The workable route is to copy the six hex values out and reassign them in your own tokens, which is where roles really live anyway.

intro: The gradient interpolator generates a fixed number of evenly spaced colors between two endpoints, returning them as discrete swatches rather than a continuous gradient.
content:
- The gradient interpolator takes two colours and a step count and returns a row of swatches, with From and To set by colour fields.
- A Steps slider runs from three to fifteen — seven by default — and the row lays out one column per step, so the palette fills the width at any count.
- Every swatch carries its hex value and a copy button, and the whole row recalculates as either colour changes.

The distinction between this and a gradient builder is the whole point of the tool, and it is easy to miss. A gradient produces a continuous ramp that the browser paints; what you get here is a list of individual colours that happen to be evenly spaced along the path between the two endpoints. That matters because a great many things cannot accept a gradient at all — chart series, heatmap scales, categorical legends, colour swatches in a design file, an array in a script. A ramp is useless for any of those, and a set of discrete steps is exactly what is needed.

The Steps slider sets the count including both endpoints, so seven steps yields the two endpoints plus five colours between them. The spacing is calculated as an even fraction along the interpolation, which means the steps are equally spaced in value but not necessarily in perceived difference — the human eye is more sensitive to change in some parts of the colour space than others, so the middle of the row can look like it moves more slowly than the ends.

That leads to the one behaviour worth knowing before you use the result. The interpolation is a straight line in the red, green and blue channels, which is the simplest possible blend and not the one that looks best. Blending a mid blue into a red runs through a muted purple in the middle — the halfway point between those two defaults lands at roughly a desaturated violet, and it is noticeably duller than either end. A perceptual interpolation through a colour space designed around how we see would keep the middle more vivid, and some tooling offers that as an option. Here, the straight line is the behaviour, and knowing it explains why some pairs seem to sag in the middle while others stay lively.

In practice, some pairs interpolate well and others do not. Colours that already sit near each other — a teal into a blue, two neighbouring greens — come out with a smooth, convincing scale. Complementary pairs, where the two endpoints are opposite on the wheel, are the ones that turn muddy in the middle, because the straight line passes near the neutral axis. If a scale looks wrong, changing an endpoint slightly usually improves it more than changing the step count.

- The set is not exported as CSS, a design token document or a chart configuration — the copy buttons take individual values, and assembling an array is a manual step.
- There is no interpolation-space option and no reversed order.
- As a way to blend two colors evenly into a usable number of steps, it does one job cleanly: ask for color steps between two colors and this is what you get, laid out and numbered — and it is the fastest way to generate color scale values when interpolate between two colors is the actual requirement rather than a smooth wash.
howTo: Set the From and To colours.
Choose a step count with the slider — the endpoints are included in the total.
Copy individual hex values from the swatches, or read the row as a scale.
Adjust an endpoint rather than the step count if the middle of the scale looks dull.
whenToUse: Use this when you need a fixed number of discrete colours between two values — a chart scale, a legend, a heatmap ramp. Use a gradient generator when you want a continuous painted ramp instead of steps. The continuous version of the same maths is the {{linear-gradient-generator|linear gradient generator}}, and a ramp that has to pass through a third colour rather than straight between two is what the {{multi-stop-gradient-builder|multi-stop gradient builder}} builds.

faqs.q: How is this different from a gradient?
faqs.a: It returns individual colours, not a painted ramp. Charts, scales, legends and design files take discrete values, which is what the numbered steps are for.

faqs.q: Do the steps include the two endpoints?
faqs.a: Yes. Seven steps means the From colour, five intermediate colours, and the To colour. Three is the minimum, and fifteen the maximum.

faqs.q: Why do some pairs look muddy in the middle?
faqs.a: The blend is a straight line through the red, green and blue channels. Complementary pairs pass close to neutral in the middle and come out duller; neighbouring hues stay smooth.

faqs.q: Can I export the whole scale?
faqs.a: Not as a block. Each swatch has its own copy button, so assembling an array or a token list is a manual step after copying the values you need.

faqs.q: Can I flip the order without changing the colours?
faqs.a: Swap the two fields — the row always runs From to To, so reversing the inputs mirrors the sequence. There is no separate reverse control, and the set of colours is the same either way.

intro: The text gradient generator writes the CSS that fills type with a horizontal two-stop gradient and previews it on a headline using the background clip text technique.
content:
- Two colour fields decide everything: a From that starts on a blue and a To that starts on a purple.
- The headline above them turns into a gradient running left to right as either field changes.
- Underneath, a code panel holds the declarations that do the work, with a copy button for the whole block.
- The angle is fixed at ninety degrees, so the gradient always travels horizontally.

The technique is a background trick rather than a text property. The element is given a linear gradient as its background, a background clip of text confines that background to the shape of the glyphs, and the text itself is made transparent so the gradient shows through. Both the standard declaration and the -webkit prefixed version are written, along with -webkit-text-fill-color and a plain transparent colour, which is why the snippet is five lines long rather than two.

One property of the approach matters in practice: the gradient is painted into the element's background box, so it stretches across the whole line rather than restarting per word. A two-word heading and a ten-word heading therefore reveal the same two colours at very different rates, and short text can look abrupt. Nothing in the interface warns about that, the preview copy is fixed, and a longer headline has to be tried in the page itself.

- Where it earns its place is display type that carries a brand moment: a hero headline, a product name, a section opener.
- Two stops are the plainest form of the idea and the easiest to keep legible, since the extremes of the ramp are colours you can test independently.
- A third colour, an angled direction and an animated background all extend the technique and none of them are available here; the snippet is a foundation to edit, and the preview is honest about that scope — one phrase, one size, one direction.

The copy is what most visitors come for. It is a plain set of declarations that drops into a stylesheet class, with no custom properties, no variables and no fallback for engines that ignore the clipping. Where those engines matter, the transparent colour line is the risk: the text becomes invisible if the clipping is unsupported, so a production headline should carry a fallback.

Legibility is the other consideration, and it is why a gradient headline css treatment deserves testing rather than trust. Contrast is judged between the gradient's colours and the surface behind the text, and a gradient that runs from strong to weak changes the answer along its length — the same headline can pass at the left edge and fail at the right.

Use it for short display type: hero headings, section labels, product names, banner titles. Two colours only, no stop positions, no angle control, no font settings and no dark-mode preview. The panel showing the effect uses one fixed phrase at one size, so the preview is a proof of the CSS rather than a layout test.

As a text gradient generator it hands over gradient text css that works the first time, and for anyone who wants css gradient text without remembering which of the four clipping declarations is required, the background clip text block is one copy away.
howTo: Set the From colour and the To colour.
Read the headline preview, which uses the same ninety-degree gradient the snippet will produce.
Copy the five declarations into a stylesheet class and apply it to short display type.
whenToUse: Use this when a heading should carry a two-colour gradient and you want the exact declarations. Use the transparent gradient generator for a fade on a surface or overlay, or the gradient generator when the gradient itself needs an angle and stop positions. When the fade belongs to a surface rather than to type, the {{transparent-gradient-generator|transparent gradient generator}} writes the scrim version, and when the ramp needs an angle or extra stops the {{multi-stop-gradient-builder|multi-stop gradient builder}} is where those controls live.

faqs.q: How does the gradient fill the letters?
faqs.a: The gradient is painted as the element's background, clipping confines that background to the glyph shapes, and the text colour is made transparent so the background shows through the letters.

faqs.q: Why are there five declarations rather than two?
faqs.a: Because the technique needs a prefixed background-clip, a prefixed text fill colour for the WebKit engines, a standard background-clip and a plain transparent colour as the fallback form.

faqs.q: Can I change the angle or add stops?
faqs.a: No. The gradient is fixed at ninety degrees with your two colours and no stop positions, so a diagonal or three-colour headline has to be edited in the copied code.

faqs.q: Does the gradient restart on each line?
faqs.a: No — it is sized to the element's background box and stretches across the whole block, so a headline that wraps shows two slices of the same single ramp.

faqs.q: What happens where background-clip is not supported?
faqs.a: The emitted block ends with a transparent text fill and a transparent colour, so an engine that ignores the clip renders the text invisible — which is why a solid colour fallback ahead of it, or a different carrier for the headline, is worth having. Email clients are the usual example.

intro: The transparent gradient generator writes a top-to-bottom CSS gradient that fades a colour into transparency, with a tall preview panel and the declaration ready to copy.
content:
- One colour field is the only control: choose a colour and a tall panel fills with a gradient that starts at that colour at the top and reaches full transparency at the bottom.
- Underneath, a code panel prints the single declaration that produced it, with a copy button for the whole value.

The gradient to transparent is written as a linear gradient at 180 degrees with two stops: your colour and the keyword transparent. One hundred and eighty degrees in CSS means top to bottom, so the fade always runs vertically downwards, and the second stop carries no position, which places it at the far end of the box. The angle and the stop placement are fixed, so the only decision the tool asks for is which colour fades out.

There is a subtlety in that keyword worth understanding. Transparent resolves to transparent black, not to your colour at zero alpha, so the interpolation runs from your colour to a clear black. Modern engines interpolate in premultiplied alpha, which removes the black and keeps the fade clean; some unusual renderers can show a grey haze partway through. Where a fade has to be exact everywhere, naming the end colour with an explicit zero alpha value is the safer form.

The dominant use is an overlay: a scrim that is opaque where it meets a caption and invisible where it meets an image. Because the output is a background value, it can be layered over anything through a background-image list or a pseudo-element, and because it reaches full transparency there is no visible seam at the bottom edge. The same shape hides the foot of a scrolling panel and softens the top edge of a coloured surface.

Choosing the colour is mostly a question of what the overlay sits on. A scrim over a photograph usually takes the hue of the image's dominant tone, so the fade reads as part of the picture rather than as a panel laid over it; a fade at the foot of a coloured card usually takes the card's own colour, which keeps the dissolve invisible until it matters. Because the gradient starts at full strength, the value at the top edge is exactly the colour chosen, and any transparency in the overlay comes from how far the ramp has travelled rather than from the colour itself.

- The fade runs top to bottom only, so a left-to-right scrim has to be re-angled in the copied code.
- There is no second colour, no stop slider and no starting opacity, so the gradient always begins at full strength — a scrim that should top out at eighty percent needs a manual edit of the colour's alpha.

There is also no image handling, no preview against real content, no separate copy button per declaration and no contrast advice for whatever will sit on the overlay. What it does, it does in one pick: as a transparent gradient generator it produces a usable fade to transparent css value, and for a quick gradient fade overlay at the foot of a card or the top of an image, the copyable css overlay fade value is the entire interaction.
howTo: Pick the colour the overlay should start from.
Check the panel, which shows the same top-to-bottom fade the CSS will produce.
Copy the declaration and apply it as a background or on a pseudo-element over the content it should scrim.
Edit the angle in the copied value if the fade needs to run horizontally instead.
whenToUse: Use this when a colour has to dissolve into whatever is behind it — image scrims, fade-outs at the edge of a scrolling panel, soft edges on a coloured surface. Use the text gradient generator when the fill belongs to type rather than to a surface. When the overlay has to carry a colour at both ends, the {{gradient-overlay-generator|gradient overlay generator}} is the two-stop version with an angle, and a fade that has to be judged against real content is what the {{overlay-color-generator|overlay color generator}} previews over an image.

faqs.q: What exactly is the generated value?
faqs.a: A linear gradient at 180 degrees from your colour to the keyword transparent, printed as a background declaration with the whole value on the copy button.

faqs.q: Why does transparent behave differently between engines?
faqs.a: The keyword resolves to transparent black rather than to your colour with zero alpha. Engines that interpolate in premultiplied alpha keep the fade clean; others can introduce a grey haze, which explicit alpha avoids.

faqs.q: Can I fade from left to right?
faqs.a: Not in the tool. The angle is fixed at 180 degrees, so a horizontal scrim means editing the angle in the copied declaration.

faqs.q: Can the fade start at partial opacity?
faqs.a: No. The gradient always begins with your colour at full strength, so a softer start requires setting an alpha value on the colour by hand.

faqs.q: Can the fade end on a second colour instead of transparency?
faqs.a: Not here — the ramp always finishes fully transparent. A wash between two colours, transparent at neither end, is what the gradient overlay generator or a gradient builder produces.

intro: The gradient reverser flips a linear gradient so the ramp runs the other way, mirroring every stop position and returning a declaration that renders the reverse of the original.
content:
- The gradient reverser takes a linear gradient written as CSS and returns the same gradient running the other way.
- Paste a value into the input field and two ramps appear one above the other — the original and the reversed version.
- Beneath them, the reversed declaration is printed with a copy button, and both panels update as you type.

What the reversal actually does is more subtle than swapping two colours, and it is the reason a naive version of this tool does not work. Each stop in a gradient carries a position along the axis, and the rendering depends on those positions rather than on the order the stops are written in. Reversing the order alone leaves every position attached to its colour, so CSS sorts the stops back into place and paints the original ramp — the text changes and the picture does not. To genuinely flip the ramp, every position has to be mirrored: a stop at zero percent moves to a hundred, one at twenty-five moves to seventy-five, and so on. Then the stops are re-ordered so they read left to right again, and the output is a mirrored ramp with an ascending, readable set of positions.

This is why a tool that appears to only reverse linear gradient stops is doing more than the phrase suggests: it is inverting the ramp, not just its source text. Mirroring the positions has a consequence worth knowing about. A stop written without an explicit position is spaced automatically by the browser, and an automatic position cannot be mirrored without first deciding what it was. The tool resolves this by computing the even spacing the browser would have used — one stop gets zero, the next a hundred, and the rest divided evenly between — and then writes every position out explicitly in the output. The reversed declaration is therefore more verbose than the input, with a percentage on every stop, which is a fair trade for a result that is unambiguous.

The gradient's head is preserved. Whatever appears before the first colour — an angle, or a direction keyword such as to right, or an interpolation directive — is carried across untouched, so only the ramp flips and never the axis. The consequence is that reversing a gradient reverses its colours but not its geometry, which is what makes the tool useful for mirroring a background: a ramp that fades to dark on the left becomes one that fades to dark on the right, with the same angle, so a pair of mirrored panels can share one gradient definition.

Only the linear form is understood. A radial or conic gradient passes through unchanged, because there is no axis to mirror in the same sense, and the output would be identical to the input. Values are also read as text rather than parsed into a full colour model, so unusual notation can defeat the pattern matching even when the browser accepts it.

Where this saves time is when a gradient exists and only its direction is wrong — a hero that fades the wrong way, a card whose tint sits on the wrong side, an icon that needs mirroring for a right-to-left layout. Rather than rebuilding the gradient by hand, or hand-editing four positions and hoping the commas survived, paste it in and take the reversed declaration. As a gradient reverser it does one small job accurately, and for reverse gradient css or flip gradient direction work the difference from a simple stop-order swap is precisely the part that makes it correct. When two panels should be mirror images of each other and share their colours, being able to invert gradient colors reliably — rather than hoping the ramp flips — is the whole value.
howTo: Paste a linear gradient value into the input field.
Compare the two panels — the original above, the reversed ramp below.
Copy the reversed declaration, which now carries an explicit position on every stop.
whenToUse: Use this when an existing gradient runs the wrong way — mirrored layouts, right-to-left interfaces, or a background that fades toward the wrong edge. Use a gradient builder when the colours themselves need changing rather than the direction. When the ramp needs rebuilding rather than flipping, the {{linear-gradient-generator|linear gradient generator}} is the builder, and a value written by hand that needs looking at is what the {{gradient-previewer|gradient previewer}} renders.

faqs.q: Why not just swap the two colours?
faqs.a: Because the positions travel with the colours. Swapping the order alone leaves CSS sorting them back into place and painting the original; the ramp only flips when each position is mirrored, which is what this tool does.

faqs.q: Why does the output include a percentage on every stop?
faqs.a: Because stops without an explicit position are spaced automatically, and an automatic position cannot be mirrored until it is known. The tool computes that spacing and writes every position explicitly.

faqs.q: Does it reverse radial or conic gradients?
faqs.a: No. Only the linear form has an axis to mirror, so any other gradient type passes through unchanged.

faqs.q: Does the angle change?
faqs.a: No. The head of the gradient — the angle or direction keyword — is preserved, so only the colour ramp flips and the axis stays where it was.

faqs.q: Does a hard stop stay hard when the gradient is reversed?
faqs.a: Yes. The two stops sharing a boundary position both mirror to the same new position, so the abrupt edge survives with the rest of the ramp — it simply lands on the other side of the element.
